tips.sources: Muzaale AD, Massie AB, Wang MC, Montgomery RA, McBride MA, Wainright JL, Segev DL (2014). Risk of end-stage renal disease following live kidney donation. JAMA, 311(6), 579-586. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2013.285141>; Mjøen G, Hallan S, Hartmann A, et al. (2014). Long-term risks for kidney donors. Kidney International, 86(1), 162-167. <https://doi.org/10.1038/ki.2013.460>; Ibrahim HN, Foley R, Tan L, et al. (2009). Long-term consequences of kidney donation. New England Journal of Medicine, 360(5), 459-469. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0804883>; Goyal M, Mehta RL, Schneiderman LJ, Sehgal AR (2002). Economic and health consequences of selling a kidney in India. JAMA, 288(13), 1589-1593. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.288.13.1589>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>
tips.caveats: Controversy exists: Ibrahim’s study used ordinary citizens as controls and found no difference in survival or ESRD risk between donors and non‑donors. Muzaale and Mjøen compared donors to equally healthy, eligible non‑donors and found markedly higher risks. The disagreement concerns the control group, not the donors themselves. All three studies agree that absolute risks remain low (30.8 per 10,000 over 15 years). Thus the key points are two: first, the remaining kidney does bear extra strain, as shown by higher rates of hypertension and proteinuria; second, these figures apply only to donors who undergo pre‑ and post‑operative screening and medical care — conditions absent for illegal kidney sellers, whose outcomes differ sharply according to Indian follow‑up data. Original studies provide only self‑reported health decline, proteinuria, hypertension, and ESRD rates; no figures on bed‑bound status are included here. Legal restrictions on organ sales, fines, and criminal penalties for relatives are detailed in Section 9, Article 22. Dialysis patients may use cross‑regional settlement and long‑term medication programs described in Section 16, Articles 1 and 2.

tips.title: Don’t pick up, disassemble, or sell unidentified metal parts; stay clear of areas marked with the clover symbol
tips.cost: No cost involved. If you see unfamiliar metal cylinders, lead containers, or parts removed from equipment, simply steer clear — don’t pick them up, take them apart, or put them in your pocket.
tips.inPlainWords: Radiation has no smell, color, or temperature. Most radioactive sources look like ordinary pieces of metal, so “it looks harmless” is not a reliable indicator. The chance of an ordinary person encountering one is extremely low — fewer than one incident occurs per 10,000 sources each year. Yet when such an encounter does happen, the consequences are irreversible. In 1987, four people died in Brazil after dismantling a radiotherapy machine from an abandoned clinic.
tips.benefit: As of 2025, roughly 178,000 radioactive sources and 355,000 radiation devices are in use nationwide. The annual rate of radiation incidents involving sources remains below one per 10,000 sources. Classification is as follows: loss, theft, or uncontrolled release of Category I or II sources constitutes a major radiation incident; Category III is a relatively serious incident. Loss or theft of Category IV or V sources, or exposure exceeding annual dose limits, counts as a minor incident. Official example: In June 2020, a γ‑ray inspection was performed during pipeline upgrades at a steel plant in Ningxia. A Category II iridium‑192 source exposed three workers to radiation; one suffered third‑degree acute skin damage, another had fourth‑degree injuries on several fingers, and a third had first‑ to second‑degree burns. All three received doses far above legal limits; both responsible firms had their radiation licenses revoked and were fined ₹9,94,700. International example: In 1987, 50.8 TBq of cesium‑137 was removed from a radiotherapy machine in Goiânia, Brazil, after the device was dismantled; the source’s protective casing was ruptured. About 112,000 people were screened; 249 showed internal or external contamination, 129 of whom required moderate to severe medical care. Four people ultimately died. (National and international statistics)
tips.sources: International Atomic Energy Agency (1988). The Radiological Accident in Goiânia. IAEA, Vienna. <https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Pub815_web.pdf>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>; Atomic Energy Regulatory Board. <https://www.aerb.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: If you ever encounter such a source, move away, note its location, do not touch it, and call 112. Reporting is mandatory to environmental, police, and health authorities. Distance and time are the only effective safeguards; plastic bags or pockets offer no protection. Devices such as X‑ray machines or CT scanners emit radiation only when powered; once turned off, they pose no residual risk. The real danger lies in the sealed radioactive source inside them. Radiotherapy machines, pipeline and boiler inspection devices, well‑logging tools, and level gauges all contain such sources, which look identical to ordinary metal parts. Therefore, never try to identify a source — simply avoid picking up, selling, or taking home any unidentified equipment parts. Workers in scrap recycling, dismantling, hardware, and construction face higher risks; they should steer clear of any area marked with the clover warning symbol. Nuclear plant leaks represent a different type of incident, with an even lower probability of affecting the general public. The primary beneficiaries of these precautions are you and anyone else present at the scene.

tips.title: When gambling leads to borrowing and persistent low mood, call Tele-MANAS on 14416, then hand your cards and payment passwords to a family member
tips.cost: No cost involved. Simply make one phone call and give your bank cards, payment passwords, and gambling apps to a family member. The hardest part is admitting that you’ve lost control over your gambling behavior.
tips.inPlainWords: Individuals who have sought treatment for gambling problems are 15 times more likely to die by suicide and 1.8 times more likely to die overall compared to their peers. Depression serves as a key warning sign for potential suicide. Therefore, if you find yourself gambling despite owing money and feeling persistently down, call 14416 (Tele-MANAS) right away.
tips.benefit: A nationwide Swedish registry study examined 2,099 individuals diagnosed with gambling disorder between 2005 and 2016. Gambling disorder is defined as an inability to control gambling habits, which negatively impacts daily life. Compared to the general Swedish population aged 20–74, these individuals showed a 1.8-fold increase in overall mortality and a 15-fold increase in suicide mortality (these figures represent standardized mortality ratios). Over the follow-up period, 67 participants died, including 21 from suicide. Depression proved to be a reliable predictor of suicide risk. In a 2023 correction, researchers reported that the suicide risk was 12.1 times higher for men and 16.1 times higher for women.
tips.sources: Karlsson A, Håkansson A. (2018). Gambling disorder, increased mortality, suicidality, and associated comorbidity: A longitudinal nationwide register study. Journal of Behavioral Addictions, 7(4), 1091–1099. <https://doi.org/10.1556/2006.7.2018.112>; Karlsson A, Håkansson A. (2023). Corrigendum. Journal of Behavioral Addictions, 12(1), 302. <https://doi.org/10.1556/2006.2023.10000>; Tele-MANAS, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://telemanas.mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: This grade is assigned because only one study exists, and it includes only individuals who sought specialist care — a group with relatively severe conditions. Consequently, the 15-fold suicide risk increase cannot be generalized to all gamblers. Handing over financial control to family members is a widely practiced approach, though lacking direct research support; thus it receives a C grade. Legal boundaries regarding gambling are outlined in Section 9, Article 13 (prohibiting bookmaking and online gambling). Whether family members should repay gambling debts incurred by a spouse is discussed in Section 8, Article 44 (such debts do not qualify as joint marital obligations). For guidance on responding to suicidal thoughts, refer to Rule 32 of this section (inform a trusted person immediately). The primary beneficiaries are the gamblers themselves; however, family members who notice warning signs can also encourage them to follow these steps.

tips.title: Men who have sex with men at high risk of HIV infection can lower their infection risk by about 70% by taking pre-exposure prophylaxis on schedule
tips.cost: This is a prescription medication, so in most places it must be paid for out of pocket. Prices range from several hundred to a few hundred rupees. Before prescribing it, doctors must test for HIV, kidney function, and hepatitis B. Follow-up tests are required every three months. The main challenge is remembering to take the pills every day without fail.
tips.inPlainWords: People who aren’t yet infected can take an antiviral drug called pre-exposure prophylaxis to protect themselves. Those who take it consistently cut their risk of infection by about 70%. On the other hand, people who take it intermittently see almost no benefit. Because it’s a prescription drug, a medical checkup is mandatory before obtaining it, and regular follow-ups are necessary thereafter.
tips.benefit: This medication is a fixed-dose combination of emtricitabine and tenofovir. In the iPrEx trial, 2,499 men who have sex with men and transgender women were assigned to either take this drug daily or receive a placebo. The group taking the medication saw a 44% reduction in infections (95% CI 15–63). Among participants whose blood tests confirmed they were taking the drug, the protective effect was even stronger. The UK’s PROUD trial involved 544 men who have sex with men; those who started treatment immediately had an 86% lower infection rate compared to those who delayed treatment for a year (90% CI 64–96). France’s IPERGAY trial evaluated on-demand dosing before and after sex; results showed an 86% drop in infections (95% CI 40–98). A meta-analysis compiled by WHO concluded that overall, the relative risk of infection dropped to 0.49 (0.33–0.73, roughly a 51% reduction). In trials where adherence exceeded 70%, the relative risk fell to 0.30 (0.21–0.45, about a 70% reduction); when adherence stayed below 40%, the relative risk was 0.95, essentially indicating no effect.
tips.sources: Grant RM, Lama JR, Anderson PL, et al. (2010). Preexposure chemoprophylaxis for HIV prevention in men who have sex with men. New England Journal of Medicine, 363(27), 2587–2599. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1011205>; McCormack S, Dunn DT, Desai M, et al. (2016). Pre-exposure prophylaxis to prevent the acquisition of HIV-1 infection (PROUD): effectiveness results from the pilot phase of a pragmatic open-label randomised trial. The Lancet, 387(10013), 53–60. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(15)00056-2>; Molina JM, Capitant C, Spire B, et al. (2015). On-demand preexposure prophylaxis in men at high risk for HIV-1 infection. New England Journal of Medicine, 373(23), 2237–2246. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1506273>; Fonner VA, Dalglish SL, Kennedy CE, et al. (2016). Effectiveness and safety of oral HIV preexposure prophylaxis for all populations. AIDS, 30(12), 1973–1983. <https://doi.org/10.1097/QAD.0000000000001145>; World Health Organization (2019). What's the 2+1+1? Event-driven oral pre-exposure prophylaxis to prevent HIV for men who have sex with men (WHO/CDS/HIV/19.8). <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/what-s-the-2-1-1-event-driven-oral-pre-exposure-prophylaxis-to-prevent-hiv-for-men-who-have-sex-with-men>
tips.caveats: The participants in these trials were primarily men who have sex with men; therefore, they are the group most encouraged to seek this treatment. Others at high risk of infection can also consult doctors to determine suitability. Prior to prescribing, it is essential to confirm that patients are not already infected; taking the medication while infected can foster viral resistance. Self-test results cannot be used as a basis for prescription. For individuals with hepatitis B, discontinuing treatment may trigger a flare-up, so testing is mandatory beforehand. WHO currently recommends on-demand dosing only for men who have sex with men engaging in sex fewer than twice a week; the regimen involves taking two tablets 2–24 hours prior to sex, followed by one tablet 24 and 48 hours afterward. Women and hepatitis B carriers must adhere to daily dosing. Trials involving on-demand dosing reported more gastrointestinal and kidney-related side effects than placebo groups; hence, regular medical checkups are indispensable. Prospective patients should call local disease control centers to identify designated HIV clinics or STD/AIDS outpatient departments offering this treatment. Importantly, this medication does not protect against sexually transmitted infections such as syphilis or gonorrhea; condoms must still be used consistently, as noted in Section 30 of this chapter. In cases where exposure has already occurred, emergency post-exposure prophylaxis is available per Section 13, Item 38 (within 72 hours). Ultimately, this treatment safeguards both the individual and their sexual partners.

tips.title: Women aged 65 and older should have a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) bone density test; postmenopausal women with osteoporosis risk factors need not wait until 65
tips.cost: A hospital DXA scan of the lumbar spine and hip takes a few minutes lying down. Out-of-pocket cost is usually ₹1,400–₹2,800, varying by region. Heel ultrasound at a checkup can screen but cannot diagnose.
tips.inPlainWords: Women aged 65 and older, and postmenopausal women with osteoporosis risk factors, should have bone density measured once. When screening starts with fracture-risk assessment and treats those at high risk, hip fractures fall by about 17%. That works out to about 5 fewer hip fractures per 1,000 people screened. Overall mortality did not change.
tips.benefit: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force 2025 recommendation is osteoporosis screening for women aged 65 and older (Grade B). Postmenopausal women under 65 at high fracture risk by assessment should also be screened (Grade B). Evidence for men is insufficient; no recommendation. The evidence review for that guidance pooled 3 randomized trials with 42,009 older European women. Screening meant assessing fracture risk first, measuring bone density in those at high risk, and treating those found high risk. Hip fractures in the screening group were about 17% lower (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.93). In absolute terms, screening avoided 5 hip fractures per 1,000 people. In the UK SCOOP trial of 12,483 women aged 70 to 85, hip fractures in the screening group were about 28% lower (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.89); mortality did not differ.
tips.sources: US Preventive Services Task Force, Nicholson WK, Silverstein M, et al. (2025). Screening for Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement. JAMA. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2024.27154>; Kahwati LC, Kistler CE, Booth G, et al. (2025). Screening for Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures: A Systematic Evidence Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2024.21653>; Shepstone L, Lenaghan E, Cooper C, et al. (2018). Screening in the community to reduce fractures in older women (SCOOP): a randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32640-5>
tips.caveats: Controversy: SCOOP's prespecified primary outcome was all osteoporotic fractures; the screening group did not show a clear reduction (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.03)—only hip fractures fell. All three trials used "assess risk, then measure bone density"; none compared bone density testing alone. The evidence review also estimated 11.8% to 24.1% overdiagnosis—people who would never have fractured from this cause in their lifetime. This item is about whether bone can survive a fall; avoiding falls themselves is item 13 (balance and leg strength)—do both. After osteoporosis is found, see item 40 (treat with medication). Primary beneficiaries are you and your parents.

tips.title: If you are diagnosed with osteoporosis, or have fractured from a minor fall, ask a doctor for osteoporosis medication and keep taking it—do not treat calcium supplements as a substitute
tips.cost: Prescription required; use continues for years. Common options include once-weekly oral drugs and once-yearly infusions. Bone density should be rechecked yearly at first, then every 1 to 2 years once stable. The hard part is continuing when you feel fine.
tips.inPlainWords: If osteoporosis is confirmed, or you have already fractured from a light fall, following a doctor's drug plan cuts hip fractures by about half and symptomatic spine fractures by a bit more than half. In older people who start yearly infusion within 90 days after hip-fracture surgery, new fractures over two years fall by about 35%. Calcium alone cannot replace these drugs.
tips.benefit: Fragility fracture means a fracture from minor trauma or everyday activity. The guideline states: "There is currently insufficient evidence that calcium supplementation alone can replace other anti-osteoporosis drug therapy." Cochrane's 2025 update on alendronate in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis or prior fracture found hip fractures about 51% lower in the treated group (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.96) and symptomatic vertebral fractures about 55% lower (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.73). The HORIZON trial enrolled 2,127 people mean age 74.5 after hip-fracture surgery; yearly zoledronic acid starting within 90 days post-op, median follow-up 1.9 years. New fractures fell from 13.9% to 8.6% (about 35% relative reduction). Death fell from 13.3% to 9.6% (about 28% relative reduction). The guideline notes about 20% of people die from complications within one year after hip fracture.

tips.title: Drill and measure ice thickness before stepping onto outdoor ice; stay off if under 15 cm (6 inches), and avoid river ice and ice fishing holes
tips.cost: The most cost-effective option is to use managed, regulated ice rinks, which incurs no extra outdoor gear cost. If you must venture onto natural outdoor ice, carry an ice auger or chisel to measure thickness, along with a pair of chest-mounted ice rescue picks (safety spikes with handles). These cost under $15–$30. Measuring every few paces as you advance requires some extra time.
tips.inPlainWords: Official safety standards require ice to be at least 15 cm (6 inches) thick before adults can safely skate on it. Guidelines in the United States and Canada set a baseline of 10 cm (4 inches) for walking or ice fishing, but that applies strictly to clear, newly formed blue ice. White snow ice is only about half as strong and requires double the thickness. On the same body of water, ice can measure a foot thick in one spot and only an inch or two just steps away, so you must measure continuously as you move.
tips.benefit: Official meteorological and water safety guidance states that ice must reach 15 cm in thickness before an adult can safely walk or skate on it, and outdoor municipal rinks are generally not cleared for public use below this threshold. Regulated natural rinks typically require a sustained thickness of 15 cm following a full week of continuous sub-zero temperatures (-8°C to 1°C) with low winds before opening. Natural outdoor ice frequently harbors holes drilled by ice anglers, which refreeze poorly and create persistent weak structural points. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (DNR) safety guidelines specify that for newly formed, clear ice: stay off if under 4 inches (10 cm); 4 inches is the minimum safe threshold for walking and ice fishing. White ice formed by melted and refrozen snow carries only about half the load-bearing strength of clear ice, requiring twice the thickness. Furthermore, ice thickness varies dramatically across a single water body—it may measure twelve inches in one area and barely one or two inches just a few feet away. Ice over moving water (streams, rivers, beneath bridges, and around culverts) is notoriously hazardous and unpredictable, and shoreline ice is often thinner than open areas. The U.S. National Weather Service sets identical thresholds: under 4 inches is unsafe for walking, fishing, or skating. The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety (CCOHS), citing Canadian Red Cross recommendations, advises a minimum of 15 cm for small groups walking or skating, and 20 cm for larger group skating gatherings. These benchmarks represent standardized physical safety engineering guidelines rather than empirical epidemiological cohorts.

tips.caveats: Official safety agencies emphasize that no outdoor natural ice is 100% safe. Meeting minimum thickness is merely a baseline qualification, never a guarantee. The early winter freeze-up and early spring thaw are the most dangerous periods. If you fall through, do not strip off your clothes: trapped air inside winter clothing provides crucial temporary buoyancy. Turn immediately toward the direction you came from, as that ice was solid enough to hold you moments earlier. Place your forearms on the ice shelf, drive your rescue ice picks into the surface, kick your legs horizontally behind you, and pull yourself out. Once out, do not stand immediately—roll horizontally away from the hole until you reach safe ground, then seek warm shelter immediately. If you witness someone else fall through, never run across the ice to grab them: follow emergency rescue protocol (shout for help, call emergency services, extend a pole, or throw a rope from a safe distance), as detailed in Chapter 13, Rule 25. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and children you accompany outdoors.

tips.title: Fit safety guards, wear safety goggles plus a full-face shield before using an angle grinder, grip firmly with both hands, and never mount toothed woodworking saw blades
tips.cost: A pair of impact-rated safety goggles and a full-face shield cost $15–$30. Checking the guard and disc before powering on, and unplugging the tool before changing discs, takes one or two extra minutes. The primary friction is resisting the temptation to remove the protective guard or operate the tool one-handed for convenience.
tips.inPlainWords: Angle grinders spin at extreme speeds (over 10,000 RPM). If an abrasive disc shatters, fragments fly out at ballistic velocity, and mounting a toothed woodworking blade causes violent, sudden kickbacks. Multiple fatal occupational accidents have documented workers mounting saw blades without guards: one severed a femoral artery, another severed a carotid artery, and neither survived. Safety guards, dual-layer eye/face protection, and a two-handed grip cost very little but prevent fatal injuries.
tips.benefit: Safety directives from the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety (CCOHS) and Workplace Health and Safety Queensland specify clear operating standards: inspect the protective guard and abrasive disc prior to operation; never use discs that are cracked, chipped, or warped. The maximum rated RPM marked on the disc must never be lower than the grinder's spindle speed. Ensure arbor size and disc diameter match manufacturer specifications precisely. Disconnect power before changing discs. Clamp workpieces securely before grinding or cutting. Wear safety glasses or goggles beneath a full-face shield. Maintain a balanced stance with both hands on the tool handles. Never use cutting discs for side-grinding, which causes structural disc failure. Do not put the tool down until the disc has come to a complete stop. Direct sparks and debris away from people and combustible materials. Queensland workplace alerts note that disc edge velocity typically reaches 70 meters per second; fitting a larger 356 mm disc onto a 230 mm tool elevates edge speed beyond 120 m/s, rapidly causing explosive disintegration. In February 2016, an Australian worker using a 230 mm angle grinder was fatally injured when projectile disc fragments penetrated his chest. Formal accident investigations in other jurisdictions record similar fatalities: in 2019, a worker in Harbin fitted a toothed circular saw blade without a guard onto an angle grinder to cut wood; the blade caught his trousers, severed his femoral artery, and caused fatal blood loss before medical aid arrived. In 2024, a renovator in Shenzhen fitted a toothed woodworking saw blade without a guard or auxiliary handle to cut a doorframe; the tool kicked back violently, severing his carotid artery and causing instant death. National and international safety standards (including GB 3883.3 and equivalent ISO/IEC norms) strictly prohibit mounting saw chains, wood-carving blades, or toothed saw blades to handheld grinders. Emergency department injury surveillance in South Korea between 2011 and 2018 tracked 8,697 injuries from high-speed rotating tools, with 4,603 cases caused by grinders: 46.4% sustained hand injuries and 23.0% suffered head/facial trauma. Compared to other rotating tools, angle grinders carried over twice the odds of severe injury (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.88–2.29). In a hospital study of 36 patients with ocular grinder trauma, 10 sustained permanent post-surgical visual acuity below 0.05 (legal blindness). An orthopedic study of 742 acute forearm and hand injuries in Turkey found angle grinders responsible for 82 cases, of which 44% occurred among retirees doing DIY home repairs. A Japanese trauma series of 15 grinder injuries found 9 were caused by improper attachments such as woodworking blades, resulting in complete finger amputations.

Ensure loose clothing, jewelry, and long hair are tied back to prevent entanglement. Grinding generates significant airborne particulates and hazardous noise; respiratory and hearing protection standards are detailed in Chapter 19, Rule 10. In the event of acute arterial laceration, immediately apply direct, continuous, heavy manual pressure, as described in Chapter 13, Rule 12. tips.title: Ask someone who seems emotionally distressed directly "Have you had thoughts of suicide?"—asking will not plant the idea or increase suicidal risk
tips.cost: Zero financial cost. Asking takes seconds, followed by taking time to listen attentively without judgment. The primary difficulty is psychological hesitation, as many people fear that mentioning suicide will introduce the thought into someone's mind.
tips.inPlainWords: The widespread fear that asking someone about suicide puts the idea in their head is directly refuted by scientific evidence. In randomized trials where high school students were asked detailed questions about suicidal ideation, participants experienced no increase in distress and no rise in suicidal thoughts compared to unasked peers. In fact, students with existing depressive symptoms reported less distress, and those with previous suicide attempts experienced a measurable decrease in suicidal ideation.
tips.benefit: In a randomized controlled trial published in JAMA involving 2,342 students across six New York high schools, classrooms were randomly assigned to complete a survey that either included or omitted explicit questions regarding suicidal ideation. Immediately following the survey and at two-day follow-up, emotional distress levels showed no statistically significant difference between groups (P = .66 and P = .41). Two days later, reported suicidal ideation was 4.7% in the surveyed group versus 3.9% in the unasked group—a statistically indistinguishable difference (P = .49). Crucially, students who were already experiencing depressive symptoms experienced significantly lower distress after being asked (P = .01), and individuals with prior suicide attempts showed a significant reduction in subsequent suicidal thoughts (P = .02). A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating 17 studies pooled 8 comparative trials of asked versus unasked participants: screening or directly inquiring about suicide did not produce any significant increase in immediate or subsequent suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, non-suicidal self-injury, or psychological distress. Across 8 randomized controlled trials evaluated, risk of bias was low or unclear. An earlier 2014 systematic review in Psychological Medicine arrived at identical conclusions: zero identified studies demonstrated an increase in suicidal ideation following direct questioning.

tips.caveats: Grade B is assigned because while trials conclusively prove that direct inquiry causes no harm, trials cannot ethically measure reductions in completed suicides. Benefit magnitude is rated Low because it reflects surrogate endpoints (ideation frequency rather than absolute mortality counts). Most trial protocols utilized clinical interviews or standardized screening questionnaires rather than informal peer conversations, though clinical guidelines generalize this finding to friends and family. If someone confirms they are having suicidal thoughts, do not leave them unattended: stay with them, connect them immediately to a crisis helpline (Tele-MANAS on 14416, or 112 if it is an emergency), and remove access to lethal means (medications, sharp objects, chemicals), as outlined in Chapter 1, Rule 25. If they express intent to harm others or have active preparations underway, immediate emergency services or hospital evaluation is necessary, as described in Chapter 8, Rule 15. The interval between acute ideation and action is often mere minutes, as noted in Chapter 1, Rule 32. Primary beneficiaries are family members, partners, friends, and colleagues.

tips.title: If you experience palpitations or an irregular heartbeat, get an ECG; if diagnosed with atrial fibrillation, consult a doctor about anticoagulants to prevent stroke, and do not substitute aspirin
tips.cost: A standard ECG costs just a few hundred rupees (under $10). Warfarin is inexpensive but requires regular blood tests (INR monitoring) to adjust the dosage. Newer direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) do not require routine blood monitoring but are more expensive. The primary challenge is maintaining daily adherence even in the absence of symptoms, and remembering to inform dentists and surgeons that you take anticoagulants before any invasive procedure.
tips.inPlainWords: Atrial fibrillation (AFib) causes the heart's upper chambers to beat chaotically, allowing blood to pool and form clots; if a clot travels to the brain, it triggers a devastating ischemic stroke. Taking doctor-prescribed anticoagulants reduces the risk of stroke by roughly 60% and lowers overall mortality by about 30%. Antiplatelet drugs like aspirin reduce stroke risk by only about 20% and cannot serve as an effective substitute. In national surveys, only a tiny fraction of high-risk patients with AFib were taking anticoagulants.
tips.benefit: AFib causes chaotic atrial quivering, leading to blood stasis and thrombus formation. The most common symptoms are palpitations, exertional fatigue, and chest discomfort, though approximately 25% of individuals report no noticeable symptoms. A single-lead ECG recording lasting >=30 seconds or a standard 12-lead ECG lasting >=10 seconds provides definitive diagnosis. A 2007 meta-analysis pooled 29 randomized controlled trials with 28,044 participants: compared to control/placebo, dose-adjusted warfarin reduced stroke by 64% (95% CI 49%–74%), whereas antiplatelet therapy (such as aspirin) reduced stroke by only 22% (95% CI 6%–35%). In direct head-to-head trials, warfarin reduced stroke by an additional 39% compared to antiplatelets. Absolute increase in major extracranial hemorrhage was under 0.3% per year. A Cochrane review evaluating 2,313 individuals with no prior stroke found warfarin lowered all-cause mortality by roughly 30% (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.50–0.94). Four landmark trials totaling 71,683 patients comparing direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) to warfarin demonstrated DOACs further reduced stroke and systemic embolism by 19% (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90) and all-cause mortality by 10% (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.85–0.95), with a 52% reduction in intracranial hemorrhage (RR 0.48), despite a 25% increase in gastrointestinal bleeding (RR 1.25). Aspirin cannot replace anticoagulation: in 5,599 patients unsuitable for warfarin, apixaban reduced stroke and systemic embolism by 55% compared to aspirin (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.32–0.62) with no significant difference in major bleeding (1.4% vs 1.2% per year; HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.74–1.75). In the BAFTA trial of 973 seniors aged >=75, warfarin reduced fatal or disabling stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, or arterial embolism by 52% compared to aspirin (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.28–0.80) with similar extracranial bleeding (1.4% vs 1.6% per year). Guidelines explicitly advise against antiplatelet monotherapy for AFib stroke prevention. ACC/AHA 2023 guidelines emphasize anticoagulation decisions depend on thromboembolic risk, regardless of whether AFib is paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent, and bleeding scores should be used to address modifiable bleeding risks rather than inappropriately withhold anticoagulation. A 2020–2021 nationwide survey found 43.8% of identified AFib cases were newly detected, and among previously diagnosed individuals, only 32.1% were using anticoagulants (19.8% in rural areas).

tips.caveats: Controverted in terms of asymptomatic population screening, though anticoagulation following diagnosis is undisputed. Evidence remains insufficient regarding whether asymptomatic individuals should undergo targeted mass screening. The USPSTF (2022) concluded evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of routine screening. The Swedish STROKESTOP trial in 75–76 year-olds found a modest 4% composite reduction in stroke, mortality, and severe bleed after ~7 years, just reaching statistical significance. The Danish LOOP study in 70–90 year-olds with implantable loop recorders detected AFib in 31.8% vs 12.2%, yet saw no significant difference in stroke rates. Thus, individuals with symptoms must be evaluated, and seniors aged >=65 should ask their doctor to check their pulse during visits, but buying dedicated commercial consumer screening monitors is unnecessary. Once on anticoagulants, do not self-administer NSAIDs like ibuprofen without medical supervision, as noted in Chapter 34, Rule 3. Anticoagulants must be taken long-term; never stop them simply because you feel fine, as described in Chapter 16, Rule 1. Hypertension is also a key risk factor, as detailed in Chapter 1, Rule 7. Individuals with AFib do not necessarily need to eliminate coffee, as discussed in Chapter 2, Rule 26. If sudden facial drooping or unilateral limb weakness develops, call emergency services immediately regardless of medication status, as detailed in Chapter 13, Rule 3. tips.title: Adults should screen once for hepatitis C antibodies; if positive, get an RNA test, and if confirmed, complete an 8- to 12-week course of oral antivirals to achieve a cure in over 95% of cases
tips.cost: An anti-HCV antibody test costs a few hundred rupees at a private laboratory and is free or nominal at a government hospital under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme. If it is positive, an HCV RNA PCR test shows whether the infection is active. Treatment is a direct-acting antiviral taken as one tablet a day for 8 to 12 weeks, free at designated government hospitals under the same programme and available as low-cost generics in the private market. The real obstacle is that a person with no symptoms rarely thinks to be tested.
tips.inPlainWords: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) can silently damage the liver for decades without causing any symptoms; a simple antibody blood test, followed by an RNA test if positive, establishes the diagnosis. For those with active infection, an 8- to 12-week course of oral antivirals clears the virus in over 95% of cases. Achieving viral clearance cuts subsequent overall mortality risk by roughly 60% and liver cancer risk by around 70%.
tips.benefit: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne viral infection with no preventive vaccine. The World Health Organization (WHO) notes that chronic hepatitis C typically remains asymptomatic for decades, often discovered only after severe liver fibrosis or cirrhosis develops. Antibody positivity reflects past exposure; an HCV RNA test is required to confirm whether active infection is present. Approximately 30% of infected individuals clear the virus spontaneously within 6 months without treatment. WHO states that direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) taken orally for 8 to 12 weeks cure almost all treated patients. An evidence review conducted for the USPSTF pooled 49 treatment trials: sustained virologic response (SVR, defined as undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks post-treatment) exceeded 95% across all genotypes, with serious adverse events occurring in only 1.9% and discontinuation due to adverse effects in 0.4%. Pooling 13 observational cohort studies, achieving SVR was associated with a 60% reduction in all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.28–0.56) and a 71% reduction in hepatocellular carcinoma (adjusted HR 0.29, 95% CI 0.23–0.38 across 20 cohorts). In a French prospective cohort of 9,895 chronic HCV patients tracked for a median of 33.4 months, DAA therapy was associated with a 52% decrease in all-cause mortality (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.33–0.70) and a 34% reduction in hepatocellular carcinoma (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.46–0.93) after adjusting for age, fibrosis stage, and alcohol consumption. Among 15,059 U.S. veterans with advanced liver disease treated with DAAs (mean follow-up 1.6 years), mortality was 2.6 deaths per 100 person-years in those achieving SVR versus 12.3 in those who did not, representing a 74% reduction in risk (adjusted HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.22–0.31). The USPSTF (2020) recommends screening all adults aged 18 to 79 (Grade B), with a single lifetime screen sufficient for most people.

tips.caveats: Controverted by Cochrane (2017), which restricts its evaluation strictly to randomized trials; finding that 138 trials were mostly short-term and assessed surrogate virologic clearance rather than clinical morbidities or long-term mortality, Cochrane asserted that whether SVR translates to reduced mortality has not yet been directly demonstrated in randomized controlled trials. Mortality and liver cancer data presented above originate from extensive prospective longitudinal observational cohorts. No trials directly randomize patients to screening versus no screening. High-risk populations designated for screening include individuals undergoing major surgery, blood transfusion, endoscopy, or hemodialysis; those with unexplained liver enzyme elevations; individuals with a history of intravenous drug use, paid plasma donation, multiple sexual partners, or men who have sex with men; people living with HIV; and regular sexual partners of HCV-infected individuals. Transmission can also occur through unsterilized tattooing, ear piercing, or shared razors and toothbrushes; casual contact (hugging, sharing utensils or cups) does not spread HCV. After successful treatment, antibody tests remain positive for life; RNA testing is required to verify cure or identify re-infection. Successful cure does not confer immunity against re-infection; active injection drug users should undergo annual RNA testing. If discovered during pregnancy, curative treatment is deferred until after delivery and cessation of breastfeeding; strict contraception is required during treatment. Patients with established cirrhosis require ongoing ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma even after viral clearance. Avoiding shared needles is detailed in Chapter 1, Rule 30. Hepatitis B requires a separate diagnostic panel, described in Chapter 1, Rule 14. HIV screening is discussed in Chapter 1, Rule 31. Guidelines caution that combining chronic HCV with excessive alcohol markedly accelerates progression to hepatic failure; alcohol limitations are detailed in Chapter 2, Rule 19. Primary beneficiaries are yourself, your spouse, and intimate partners.

tips.title: Ventilate septic tanks, sewer manholes, cesspools, vegetable cellars, and fermentation tanks before entering; if someone collapses inside, never jump in after them—call emergency services immediately
tips.cost: Zero financial cost. Opening all covers and ventilation shafts and waiting upwind takes some extra time. Household septic tanks are safest when emptied by licensed professional service teams with proper equipment. The main difficulty is overcoming the instinct to rush in when a companion or family member collapses.
tips.inPlainWords: Septic tanks, manholes, cesspools, and sealed vegetable cellars accumulate lethal concentrations of toxic gases (like hydrogen sulfide) and suffer severe oxygen deficiency, knocking an entrant unconscious within seconds. Across official industrial accident registries, a single worker collapses, and coworkers or relatives rush in consecutively to rescue them, only to die alongside them. Official statistics show over half of all confined space fatalities are would-be rescuers. If someone collapses inside, never enter: call emergency dispatch (such as 119 and 120) immediately.
tips.benefit: A "confined space" refers to enclosed or partially enclosed spaces not designed for continuous human occupancy, including septic tanks, sewage pits, manholes, storage cellars, and industrial vats. Accidents involving blind, unequipped rescue attempts accounted for 87.4% of incidents and 86.8% of deaths. The Ministry's 2020 Safety Guidance Manual highlighted that nearly 80% of confined space disasters saw casualties escalate due to impromptu, unprotected rescue attempts, and over 50% of total fatalities were would-be rescuers. In 2019, during a sewage pit cleaning at a paper mill in Dongguan, three workers collapsed from hydrogen sulfide; six workers entered consecutively to attempt a rescue, resulting in seven deaths. In 2020 at a noodle manufacturing plant in Jiaozuo, one worker fell into a fermentation tank; five coworkers rushed in to assist, resulting in six deaths. The U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) investigated 70 fatal confined space incidents between 1983 and 1993 involving 109 deaths: 39 victims (36%) entered specifically to rescue others, and only 4 of those 39 were trained emergency personnel. A 1986 NIOSH alert estimated that approximately 60% of confined space fatalities were would-be rescuers. Safety manuals explain that while hydrogen sulfide smells like rotten eggs at low levels, high concentrations rapidly cause olfactory paralysis—the human nose completely loses the ability to smell it. Concentrations exceeding 1,000 mg/m³ cause instantaneous "knockdown" and death within seconds. Similarly, extreme carbon dioxide concentrations induce loss of consciousness in seconds. Emergency guidelines strictly mandate: if local personnel lack breathing apparatus and retrieval gear, immediately call 112/120; "under no circumstances should forced entry be attempted." Rescuing an occupant from the outside requires that the entrant was already wearing a full-body harness attached to an external retrieval winch line. Ministerial Order No. 13 mandates that industrial work strictly follow the rule: "ventilate first, test next, enter last." Unventilated subterranean vegetable cellars also pose acute asphyxiation risks because stored root vegetables consume oxygen and release dense carbon dioxide; authorities advise opening all cellar hatches for prolonged natural ventilation, testing air, wearing safety ropes, and maintaining surface observers before entry.

tips.caveats: Grade C is assigned because data stem from occupational casualty registries and safety engineering codes rather than clinical intervention trials. Benefit magnitude is rated Moderate: while the event outcome is frequently fatal (often taking multiple lives at once), exposure is concentrated among individuals who access these subterranean structures. Common domestic encounters include cleaning septic or biogas tanks and descending into winter vegetable storage cellars. Never rely on smell to judge atmospheric safety; absence of odor does not mean toxic gas is absent. If assigned by an employer to enter shafts or tanks without mechanical ventilation, gas testing equipment, continuous surface monitoring, or safety harnesses, workers have the statutory right to refuse, as detailed in Chapter 19, Rule 10. If someone collapses inside, shout for help and dial emergency dispatch (119 and 120); external actions are limited to removing covers and using fans or blowers from outside. Once an unconscious victim is extracted to fresh air, check for breathing and initiate chest compressions if breathing is absent, as outlined in Chapter 13, Rule 1. The protocol remains identical whether the victim is a coworker, neighbor, or stranger, adhering to the same safety boundary as Chapter 13, Rule 25 (do not jump into water if you see someone drowning). Carbon monoxide risks from indoor fuel burning are covered in Chapter 1, Rule 3. Primary beneficiaries are yourself (as the prospective rescuer) and coworkers or family members.

tips.title: Adults aged 45 and older living in high-incidence areas for gastric and esophageal cancers, with family history, or tested positive for H. pylori, should undergo screening gastroscopy
tips.cost: A standard diagnostic gastroscopy costs a few hundred rupees ($40–$80); painless gastroscopy with sedation adds a few hundred rupees, varying by region. Patients must fast overnight, occupying half a day. Sedated procedures require an accompanying adult. The primary physical discomfort is the passing of the endoscope through the throat during unsedated procedures.
tips.inPlainWords: For individuals aged 45 and older in high-risk categories for gastric or esophageal cancers, undergoing gastroscopy is associated with a roughly 50% lower mortality from these cancers in observational studies. However, people who proactively schedule screenings generally maintain healthier lifestyles, which inflates observational estimates; in rigorous randomized community trials, the reduction in esophageal cancer mortality was approximately 20%, falling within the margin of error. Clinical guidelines advise against routine gastroscopy for average-risk individuals outside high-risk groups.
tips.benefit: Screening is recommended between ages 45 and 74, using endoscopy as the primary modality, generally performed every 5 years. The 2022 national guidelines explicitly advise against population screening outside high-risk groups. Screening uptake was 33.53%; on an intention-to-treat basis across the entire invited population, mortality decreased by 31% (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.66–0.72). In a 10-year non-randomized village screening study in a high-incidence esophageal cancer region, cumulative esophageal squamous cell carcinoma mortality was 3.35% in the screened cohort versus 5.05% in the control cohort. In the Korean National Cancer Screening Program, undergoing endoscopy was associated with a 47% reduction in gastric cancer mortality (adjusted OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.51–0.56), whereas upper GI barium series showed no significant benefit (OR 0.98); protection increased with frequent screening. A meta-analysis pooling 10 Asian studies found endoscopic screening was associated with a 40% reduction in gastric cancer mortality (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.49–0.73), without significant change in cancer incidence. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis adjusted for healthy screener bias: among individuals who actually received endoscopic screening, gastric cancer mortality was 48% lower (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.39–0.79), but on an intention-to-screen programmatic basis across all invited individuals, the reduction was non-significant (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.71–1.28).

tips.caveats: Controverted in literature. Most evidence demonstrating mortality reduction stems from observational cohorts comparing volunteers who attend screening against non-participants; self-selected participants tend to have higher health consciousness, exaggerating estimated benefits. The 2023 Lancet Regional Health meta-analysis classified study bias risk as moderate to serious. In the cluster-randomized ESECC trial, 9-year mortality differences did not reach statistical significance. The 2022 national guidelines cite potential harms including overdiagnosis, false positives, missed diagnoses, hemorrhage, perforation, cardiopulmonary complications, aspiration pneumonia, and infection. Overdiagnosis refers to detecting indolent early lesions that would never cause symptoms during a lifetime. For those who cannot tolerate standard endoscopy, clinical protocols specify procedures can be performed under sedation or anesthesia. Individuals aged >=45 with positive Helicobacter pylori are categorized as high gastric cancer risk. Eradication of H. pylori is detailed in Chapter 1, Rule 23, but eradication does not eliminate the need for endoscopic screening—both are required. Upper GI barium swallow, serum pepsinogen alone, tumor biomarker panels, and PET-CT scans are not recommended for screening. Commercial tumor marker panels are reviewed in Chapter 6, Rule 7. Those diagnosed with chronic atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, or intraepithelial neoplasia require shorter endoscopic surveillance intervals per gastroenterologist guidance. Residents can inquire with local CDCs or county hospitals regarding whether their area qualifies as high-incidence. Anyone already experiencing alarm symptoms like dysphagia, hematemesis, or melena requires urgent diagnostic medical care rather than screening, as outlined in Chapter 34, Rule 6. Avoiding scalding hot tea is detailed in Chapter 2, Rule 30. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and aging parents.

tips.title: Consume soaked black fungus (wood ear) and silver ear within the same meal without storing overnight, eat fresh wet rice noodles on the day of purchase, and never make fermented cornmeal at home
tips.cost: Zero financial cost. Soak only the quantity of wood ear or silver ear needed for a single meal, and discard any leftovers. Buy only enough fresh wet rice noodles for same-day consumption. The primary difficulty is reluctance to discard surplus soaked fungus, and regional culinary habits of preparing homemade fermented cornmeal dishes (such as suantangzi).
tips.inPlainWords: Black fungus and tremella (silver ear) soaked for extended periods, improperly stored fresh wet rice noodles, and home-fermented corn flour products can be contaminated by Burkholderia gladioli pathovar cocovenenans, producing bongkrekic acid—a lethal bacterial toxin. Bongkrekic acid cannot be broken down by 100°C boiling or pressure cooking, and there is no known medical antidote.
tips.benefit: By food category: 9 outbreaks involved homemade fermented corn flour products, causing 33 deaths; 5 outbreaks involved wet rice noodles, causing 7 deaths; and 3 outbreaks involved soaked black fungus, resulting in 5 illnesses and 3 deaths. In 2020 nationwide food poisoning fatalities (143 deaths), bongkrekic acid caused 12 deaths, ranking behind wild poisonous mushrooms (80 deaths) and methanol (14 deaths). Market regulation safety alerts confirm bongkrekic acid is heat-stable and resistant to 100°C boiling and pressure cooking; currently no specific antidote exists. In Guangdong Province, regulatory mandates enacted in 2018 required wet rice noodles to be prepackaged, sealed in small portions, and clearly labeled with expiration dates; post-implementation surveillance showed average annual poisoning cases dropped from 6.25 to 0.5.
tips.sources: Liu Z et al. (2026). Controlling the Storage Time Is an Effective Measure to Reduce the Risk of Bongkrekic Acid Poisoning Caused by Wet Rice Noodles. Foodborne Pathogens and Disease, 23(7), 468-472. <https://doi.org/10.1089/fpd.2024.0131>; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: In October 2020 in Jidong County, Heilongjiang Province, family members consumed homemade fermented cornmeal noodles (suantangzi) for breakfast; all 9 individuals who ate the food died (100% case-fatality). Dried black fungus requires only 1 to 2 hours of cold-water soaking; market guidelines stipulate soaking should never exceed 8 hours. If soaked fungus feels slimy, loses elasticity, gives off a sour or unpleasant odor, or if soaking water becomes turbid, discard the entire batch immediately. If symptoms like vomiting, dizziness, or profound weakness appear after eating, induce vomiting immediately, preserve remaining food samples, and seek urgent hospital emergency care. Anyone who consumed the same food must undergo medical evaluation even if currently asymptomatic. Wild toxic mushrooms are covered in Chapter 1, Rule 5.
